chapter.title: Signal, Delayed
chapter.sub: Phones get the alert in five seconds. The signs on the quad take ninety-three.
chapter.status: **DRAFT** · scripted from the series plan · IDs provisional

items.text: SEASON 5 · EPISODE 7 · DRAFT  Boundary · Officer Delgado, Maya, Tomas and the emergency manager · Level L4 · Intermediate support  At the noon test of the campus emergency alerts, phones buzz in five seconds. The signs on the quad keep showing lunch specials for a minute and a half.  ⚑ RV-132: every alert belongs to the emergency manager. RV-133: timings illustrative. Some choices run on a clock.

items.title: Signal, Delayed
items.stakes: A shelter message reaches phones in five seconds and the quad's signs in ninety-three. For some people on that quad, the sign is the only alert there is.
items.reward: Every kiosk inside the emergency manager's budget, proven by her test. Every word still hers.

objectives.text: Get the kiosks onto the push path
Look closer: two things about the quad

items.rumor: Phones are fast. Signs are slow. The same message. Where does it wait?

items.alt: The quad at noon: the signage kiosk on the path still shows the lunch menu. A callout on the right: phones got the TEST shelter alert in 5 seconds. A callout on the left: the kiosk, 47 seconds later, still showing lunch.
items.caption: 12:00:47. Every phone on the quad knows. The only sign on the quad doesn't.

lines.text: Ninety-three seconds. In a real one, that's a student walking into whatever we're warning about.
Then let's find out where it waits. With her test, not ours.

items.alt: Delgado and Maya beside the kiosk on the quad a few minutes after the test.

bubbles.text: Ninety-three seconds to the kiosks. Phones: five. The test log doesn't lie.
Then let's find out where it waits.

items.prompt: Could you just put ‘SHELTER IN PLACE’ on one sign for a second? To see how fast it goes?

options.label: “No — I don't write alerts, even as a test. Can we ask Ines for a timestamped TEST in her two o'clock window?”
options.reply: Fair. She'd have both our badges. I'll call her.

options.label: “Sure, just one.”
options.reply: …Actually, no. Somebody would photograph it. Forget I asked.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #48 · AVERY'S LENS  Every channel is somebody's only channel  An alert is as fast as its slowest path to the people who depend on that path.  Phones had the test in five seconds. The kiosks — the only alert a deaf student crossing the quad would see — took ninety-three.

items.prompt: 12:10. Delgado wants to know where the 93 seconds go. How do you measure it?
items.risk: A real alert that arrives after the danger.
timeout: Delgado goes back to his office without numbers.
The next test will be ninety-three seconds too.

hints.text: Whose words, and whose test window?

options.result: Someone photographs it. By 12:20 it's on three group chats.
options.fail: Never write, edit or send an alert — not even as a test.

options.consequence: Her message, her window; your stopwatch.

options.label: Reboot the kiosks
options.result: They come back and poll every 60 s, as before.

options.label: Tell Delgado signs aren't an alert channel
options.result: Farah hears about it by 1 p.m.
options.consequence: For some people the sign is the only channel.

items.alt: System View of the 2 p.m. TEST, stage by stage as a bar: console 2 s, hub hold 30 s, the kiosks' polling 60 s, screen 1 s — 93 s in total. Below, the phones' bar: 5 s.
items.caption: The biggest term isn't the network. It's the kiosks asking ‘anything new?’ once a minute.

items.title: From Mira
items.body: Farah forwards a text from Mira, sent at 12:01: *Was that alert real? My phone was in my bag. The sign by the fountain said pasta.* Farah's note: *Students who can't hear the siren look at the signs. Please make them first, not last.*

items.title: The push path was already there.
items.body: Indoor screens got the same TEST in 33 seconds: the signage alert gateway pushes to them the moment the hub releases it. The eighteen outdoor kiosks never get the push — so they fall back to asking every 60 seconds. They can't reach the gateway at all.
items.label: Test: what's different about the kiosks?

items.alt: Tomas's switch view: the alert gateway and the library screen on VLAN 410 SIGNAGE; the quad kiosks on VLAN 500 BUILDING SYSTEMS, next to the heating controller.

bubbles.text: The contractor put them with the sprinkler and heating controllers. ‘Outdoor equipment.’

lines.text: The contractor put them on building systems because ‘they're outdoor equipment, like the sprinkler controllers’.
They're the part of the emergency system people look at.

items.sub: Intermediate · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Maya and Delgado beside a board. Total latency is the sum of every stage: the console, the hub, the player's polling, the screen. Two, thirty, sixty and one second… ninety-three seconds before a shelter message shows. The polling term is the biggest. That's the one we remove — with your approval.

items.caption: Intermediate: the formula and what every letter means. The arithmetic is yours.

items.text: 📗 FIELD NOTES · INTERMEDIATE  Terms   Emergency notification   Latency   Signage player   Formula and variables   ƒ FORMULA · Total latency  L total  = L 1  + L 2  + … + L n    L 1  … L n   the delay each stage adds, ms  L total   end-to-end delay, ms     ƒ FORMULA · Time budget  T = Σ (count × time each)   count  how many of each task  time each  minutes or seconds per task — keep units the same

items.title: Alarms you can see
items.body: In 1990 the Americans with Disabilities Act became law in the United States, and the accessibility guidelines that followed required visible alarms — flashing strobes — alongside audible fire alarms in public buildings. The idea was simple: an alert that only some people can perceive is not an alert for everyone. Every sign on a campus quad inherits that rule.

items.prompt: 3:30. You know why the kiosks poll. What do you ask for?
unknown: What else is on that VLAN
items.risk: Friday's test — and a real alert before it.
timeout: The plan waits in your drafts.

hints.text: What change fixes the kiosks without touching anyone else's protection?

options.label: Ask Tomas to open the firewall between building systems and signage
options.result: Tomas: “Heating controllers stay isolated. Move the kiosks, not the wall.”
options.consequence: Weakens a boundary that protects building systems.

options.label: Bring Tomas the stage timings and a VLAN plan: kiosks onto SIGNAGE, building systems untouched
options.result: Tomas moves all eighteen that evening. Push reaches every kiosk.
options.consequence: Evidence to the owner; the change fits the boundary.

options.label: Set the kiosks to poll every second
options.result: Four hundred players hammer the content server; indoor screens freeze.
options.consequence: Faster polling is still polling — and it breaks the server.

options.label: Ask the contractor to come back next quarter
options.result: Three more monthly tests at 93 seconds.
options.consequence: Too slow for a life-safety path.

items.label: **Fix it:** prepare Tomas's change — put the kiosks where alerts can reach them.

items.title: Thirty seconds on purpose.
items.body: With push, the kiosks drop to 2 + 30 + 1 + 1 = 34 seconds — and now the hub's 30-second hold is the biggest term. It isn't a bug. The emergency manager set it after a March false alarm named the wrong building: corrections must beat distribution. It's hers.
items.label: Test: why might she want it — and what do you do?

items.prompt: Wednesday. The hold is now 30 of the kiosks' 34 seconds. What do you do?
items.risk: Deciding a life-safety trade-off that isn't yours.
timeout: She never sees the numbers her decision needs.

hints.text: Whose trade-off is speed against corrections?

options.label: Change the hold yourself — the old integration login still works
options.result: Okoro finds the change in her audit log by lunch.
options.consequence: Her system, her decision — and a login that should be gone.
options.fail: Never change an emergency system you don't own.

options.label: Show the emergency manager the stage timings and ask what hold she wants for signage — and tell her the old login still works
options.result: Okoro: “Signs can be retracted in seconds. Five for signage; thirty for the rest. And thank you — revoking that login now.”
options.consequence: Your numbers, her decision — and a boundary closed.

options.label: Ask Delgado to get it changed
options.result: Delgado forwards your email without the numbers.
options.consequence: The owner needs the evidence directly.

options.label: Leave it — 34 s is better than 93
options.result: It is. It's also not her decision you've made.

items.alt: The AV office: Maya on a video call with Ines Okoro, the campus emergency manager, whose face fills the screen.

bubbles.text: Two, thirty, one, one. Your hold is thirty of the thirty-four. It's your call.
Five for signage — signs can be pulled back fast. Thirty for the rest. And revoke that old login today.

items.title: Hold: 30 s · set by I. Okoro
items.body: The hold has a note beside it: *30 s — after the March false alarm (wrong building). Corrections must beat distribution.* Maya reads it twice. A fast wrong alert is its own emergency. Her numbers are for Okoro's decision, not against it.

items.label: **Route it:** from her console to the quad.
**Service Mode:** run the noon test yourself.

items.alt: System View of Friday's noon TEST: console 2 s, hub hold 5 s, push 1 s, screen 1 s — 9 s in total, beside the phones' 5 s.
items.caption: Nine seconds, stage by stage, with her test and her words.

items.alt: Friday noon on the quad: the kiosk shows the emergency manager's red THIS IS A TEST template. Delgado and Maya watch it.

bubbles.text: Nine seconds. I walked here slower than that.

items.alt: Early morning. Maya, still in a hoodie, answers her phone: TESS, REGIONAL HUB, 6:41 a.m.

bubbles.text: Maya. The hub lost its clock at 2:14. Everything that takes time from us has been drifting all night — including your campus. Remember Cal's fourteenth?

items.caption: Next: *One Clock.*

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  Add every stage of an alert path and attack the biggest term — but only the terms that are yours. Push beats polling. Every word, every hold and every test belongs to the emergency manager; you measure and carry.
REFLECTION (optional)  · For some people on the quad, the sign was the only alert. Which of your systems is somebody’s only channel?
